description_full: United Natural Foods, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, distributes natural, organic, specialty, produce, and conventional food and non-food products in the United States and Canada. It operates in three segments: Natural, Wholesale, and Retail. The company distributes grocery and general merchandise, perishables, frozen food, wellness and personal care items, bulk and foodservice, home, health and beauty care, pharmacy, pet food, produce, meat, dairy, and organic/non-GMO products under the essential everyday, shoppers value, wild harvest, field day, stone ridge creamery, equaline, culinary circle, super chill, arctic shores seafood company, koyo, and woodstock brands. It also engages in the manufacture of natural and organic snack food; importing, roasting, packaging, and distributing of nuts, dried fruit, seeds, trail mixes, granola, natural and organic snack items, and confections under the Woodstock Farms Manufacturing brand; and operation of grocery and liquor stores under the Cub Foods and Shoppers brands. In addition, the company provides shelf and planogram management, retail store support, pricing strategy, shelf tags, electronic payments and coupon processing, store layout and design, equipment sourcing and procurement, point-of-sale hardware and software, network and data hosting solutions, consumer convenience services, automation tools, sustainability services, and administrative back-office solutions; consumer and trade marketing programs; and programs to support suppliers in understanding its markets. Further, it offers web and digital marketing services, such as websites, digital coupon and loyalty programs, mobile applications, e-commerce, and circular programs; and various supply chain, digital, and professional services. It serves grocery chains and retailers. United Natural Foods, Inc. was founded in 1976 and is headquartered in Providence, Rhode Island.

financial_summary: United Natural Foods, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $2.7B market cap on $31.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +14% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 3% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 15% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $323M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 6.43× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 1.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 3.3% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

It accounts for 0.9% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 1.14, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.23 vs 5y 1.27), so read it loosely.
About $25.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The stock trades 53% below its DCF fair value of $96.23, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 87%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $65.13 to $142 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Consumer Defensive peers: cheaper on P/FCF 8.4 vs 16.0, richer on P/E 33.8 vs 18.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 31% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 11.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $53.00 on average, 17% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.00).
It runs a 15% gross margin and converts 1% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9.
ROE of 5% is amplified by 4.4x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($37.0M of cash against $1.8B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.0% over 3 years, 2.9% over 5 years and 13.9% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 26%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 1.2% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (0.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 4, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 18.7% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.3%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (1.8% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 0.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 23,431 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 2.6x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 13.7% a year.
That works out to $14K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.3M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
